usage: 끓이다 'boil (something)' is the standard verb for making stew, not 만들다
the stew comes to a boil
intransitive 끓다 — the pot bubbles on its own
name + 주세요 is how you order any stew
그릇 is the counter for a bowl/portion of stew or rice
examples: 저는 김치찌개를 좋아해요.
I like kimchi jjigae.
simple statement of taste — 를 marks the object
찌개가 아직 끓고 있으니까 조심하세요.
The stew is still boiling, so be careful.
everyday warning at the table; -고 있다 = ongoing action
여기 된장찌개 둘이서 같이 먹을게요.
We'll share one doenjang jjigae between the two of us.
real ordering line — 찌개 is communal, eaten from one pot
nuance: 찌개 is a thick, salty, intensely flavored stew with just enough liquid to spoon over rice, simmered and served bubbling in one earthenware pot that everyone at the table dips into together. The key contrast is 찌개 vs 국: a 국 is a clear, light, soup-like broth you can drink by the bowl (each person gets their own), while a 찌개 is denser, saltier, packed with solid ingredients, and meant to be shared. It is named after its base — 김치찌개, 된장찌개, 부대찌개 — and habitually pairs with 끓이다 'to boil/cook' and 끓다 'to come to a boil'. The big pitfall for English speakers is the verb: you 먹다 'eat' a 찌개, never 마시다 'drink' it (you only 마시다 a thin broth), and you cook it with 끓이다, not 만들다. Do not call it 'soup' on a menu either — that flattens the whole distinction Koreans care about.

Calling 찌개 a 'soup' and lumping it with 국 — a 국 is light and individually served, while 찌개 is dense, salty, and shared from one pot.
Using 만들다 'make' for cooking it; Koreans specifically say 찌개를 끓이다 'boil up a stew', because the cooking method is defined by simmering.

usage: 먹다 'eat', not 마시다 — even though it's soupy, the rice makes it a meal you eat
뜨겁다 = hot to the touch/temperature, the typical comment on a steaming bowl
examples: 국밥 한 그릇 주세요.
One bowl of gukbap, please.
simplest ordering line; 그릇 is the natural counter
술 마신 다음 날엔 국밥이 최고예요.
The day after drinking, gukbap is the best.
everyday hangover context — 해장 culture
국물에 밥을 말아서 드세요.
Mix the rice into the broth and eat.
real server's tip; 말다 'to put rice into soup' is the exact verb
nuance: 국밥 is literally 국 'soup' + 밥 'rice' — a hot bowl in which rice is either pre-mixed into the broth (토렴) or served alongside to add yourself, eaten fast and cheap as a complete one-bowl meal. It differs from a plain 국 in that 국밥 is a whole meal (rice included), whereas 국 is just the soup component of a larger spread. The defining verb to learn is 말다 'to put/swirl rice into soup' — 밥을 국에 말다 — which has no clean English equivalent and trips learners up. 국밥 is the classic 해장 'hangover-cure' food, and Busan's 돼지국밥 (pork) is nationally famous. Pitfall: even though it looks like soup, you say 국밥을 먹다 'eat gukbap', not 마시다 'drink', because the rice makes it food, not a beverage — and don't forget the counter 그릇 when ordering a single bowl.

Ordering '국밥 하나' and stopping there in a sit-down place; the natural, polite phrasing uses the bowl counter: 국밥 한 그릇 주세요.

english: deopbap; rice topped with a dish
usage: 시키다 'order (food)' — the casual verb diners actually use
맛있다 'be delicious' is an adjective; no 'be' verb needed
하나 'one (thing)' works as a quick counter when ordering
examples: 바쁠 때는 덮밥을 자주 먹어요.
When I'm busy I often eat deopbap.
simple habit; one-bowl food = fast
오징어덮밥은 매콤해서 인기가 많아요.
Squid deopbap is popular because it's spicy.
everyday reason with -아서 'because'
밥 위에 소스까지 부어 주세요.
Please pour the sauce over the rice too.
real request; 위에 'on top of' captures the 'covered' image
nuance: 덮밥 comes from the verb 덮다 'to cover' + 밥 'rice' — literally 'covered rice' — a single bowl where a saucy cooked topping (spicy pork, squid, egg, etc.) is laid over white rice and eaten together. The sharp contrast to master is 덮밥 vs 비빔밥: in a 덮밥 the topping sits ON the rice and you eat down through the layers, while in a 비빔밥 'mixed rice' everything is vigorously stirred together (비비다 'to mix') before eating. Common members are 제육덮밥, 오징어덮밥, and 규동-style 소고기덮밥. Two pitfalls hit English speakers: first, do not add a plural -들 because English says 'toppings' — Korean nouns stay unmarked for number; second, do not stir a 덮밥 like a 비빔밥 unless you want to blur the very distinction the name encodes. Order it casually with 시키다, the everyday verb for ordering dishes.

mistakes: Mixing up 덮밥 (topping laid over rice) with 비빔밥 (everything stirred together) — the names literally mean 'covered' vs 'mixed', and Koreans eat them differently.
Adding a plural ending like 토핑들 because English pluralizes 'toppings'; Korean leaves the noun unmarked — 덮밥 위의 재료 is fine.
Using only 만들다 'make' when ordering out — diners say 덮밥을 시키다 'order a deopbap', since 시키다 is the verb for ordering prepared food.

usage: to fry up the fried rice
볶다 'to stir-fry' is the root verb and the one cooks use
만들다 'make' for the general home-cooking sense
김치 + 볶음밥; the most common kind
examples: 남은 밥으로 볶음밥을 해요.
I make fried rice with leftover rice.
simple home use; 하다 stands in for 만들다 casually
김치볶음밥에 계란프라이를 올려 먹어요.
I eat kimchi fried rice with a fried egg on top.
everyday combo; 올리다 'to put on top'
고기 다 먹고 볶음밥 볶아 주세요.
After the meat, please fry up some rice for us.
real BBQ-restaurant line; staff fry it on the grill
nuance: 볶음밥 is 볶음 'stir-frying' (from 볶다 'to stir-fry') + 밥 'rice' — rice tossed in a hot oiled pan with bits of kimchi, vegetables, or meat until it's separated and a little toasty. The contrast learners need is 볶음밥 vs 비빔밥: 볶음밥 is cooked WITH heat — the rice is fried — whereas 비빔밥 is raw-assembled and just stirred cold, no pan. The signature collocation is the cognate-verb pair 볶음밥을 볶다 'stir-fry the fried rice', and at Korean BBQ places staff famously 볶다 it right on the grill at the end of the meal. 김치볶음밥 is the everyday home version. Pitfall: English speakers reach only for 만들다 'make', but a Korean cook will say 볶다 'stir-fry' for the actual action — and watch the spelling/spacing, it is one word 볶음밥, not 볶음 밥.

mistakes: Confusing 볶음밥 (fried in a pan with heat) with 비빔밥 (cold-mixed, no cooking) — only 볶음밥 involves the stir-fry verb 볶다.
Saying only 볶음밥을 만들어요 and never 볶아요; locals use the cognate verb 볶다 'stir-fry' for the cooking action itself.
Writing it as two words 볶음 밥; it is a single fixed compound, 볶음밥, with no space.

usage: 맵다 'be spicy' — many 볶음 dishes are red-pepper based
볶음 + 반찬; small 볶음 dishes serve as sides
examples: 저는 오징어볶음을 좋아해요.
I like stir-fried squid.
simple preference statement
제육볶음은 밥이랑 먹어야 맛있어요.
Stir-fried pork is best eaten with rice.
everyday pairing; -아야 'only if/must'
엄마가 반찬으로 멸치볶음을 자주 해 주세요.
Mom often makes anchovy stir-fry as a side dish.
real home context; small 볶음 = banchan
nuance: 볶음 is the noun made from 볶다 'to stir-fry' (the -(으)ㅁ ending turns a verb into 'the act/result of'), so it names any dish defined by stir-frying and almost always rides on the main ingredient: 오징어볶음, 제육볶음, 낙지볶음, 멸치볶음. Contrast it with 무침 'a dressed/tossed dish', which is seasoned raw without heat, and with 조림 'a braised dish', which is simmered long in sauce — all three are cooking-method suffixes, and 볶음 specifically means 'pan-fried in oil over high heat'. Big 볶음 dishes (제육볶음) are mains; tiny ones (멸치볶음) are everyday 반찬 side dishes. Pitfall: 볶음 rarely stands alone in speech — saying just '볶음 주세요' sounds incomplete; you almost always front it with the ingredient. And keep the noun 볶음 distinct from the verb 볶다 you conjugate (볶아요/볶았어요).

Assuming 볶음 means raw or tossed — that's 무침; 볶음 is specifically stir-fried in oil over heat.

usage: 새콤하다 'pleasantly sour' — many 무침 use vinegar
cognate verb 무치다 'to dress by hand'
examples: 오늘 반찬은 시금치무침이에요.
Today's side dish is seasoned spinach.
simple banchan statement
오이무침이 새콤해서 입맛이 돌아요.
The tangy cucumber muchim revives my appetite.
everyday taste comment; -아서 'because'
엄마가 콩나물을 조물조물 무쳐요.
Mom dresses the bean sprouts by hand, kneading them.
real cooking scene; 조물조물 mimetic for hand-tossing
nuance: 무침 comes from 무치다 'to dress/toss (food) by hand with seasonings', so a 무침 is vegetables or seafood mixed with salt, sesame oil, vinegar, garlic, or chili — by hand, usually with no cooking — and served cool as a 반찬 side dish: 콩나물무침, 시금치무침, 오이무침. The crucial contrast is 무침 vs 볶음: a 무침 is dressed RAW (or with just-blanched veg) and eaten cold, while a 볶음 is stir-fried in oil over heat. The signature cognate phrase is 무침을 무치다 'to dress the muchim by hand', often with the mimetic 조물조물 'kneading lightly'. Pitfall for English speakers: 무침 is normally served at room temperature or cold, so don't expect a hot dish — and the action is 무치다 'toss/dress by hand', not 섞다 'stir/mix with a tool'; the hands-on kneading is the point.

mistakes: Expecting 무침 to arrive hot — it's dressed and served cool or at room temperature, unlike the stir-fried, heated 볶음.
Confusing 무침 (raw, hand-dressed) with 볶음 (stir-fried in oil) — 무친다 means tossing by hand, no pan involved.
Using 섞다 'mix with a spoon' for the action; the precise verb is 무치다 'dress/toss by hand', often described as 조물조물 kneading.

usage: 짭짤하다 'pleasantly salty' — the typical 조림 flavor
cognate verb 조리다 'simmer down in sauce'
장 'soy sauce' + 조림; a keep-well banchan
examples: 반찬으로 감자조림이 나왔어요.
Braised potatoes came as a side dish.
simple banchan statement
장조림은 짭짤해서 밥반찬으로 좋아요.
Soy-braised beef is salty, so it's good with rice.
everyday reason; -아서 'because'
생선조림을 약한 불에 천천히 조려요.
I braise the fish slowly on low heat.
real cooking method; 약한 불 'low flame'
nuance: 조림 is from 조리다 'to braise/simmer down', a dish cooked low and slow in a seasoned (usually soy-sauce-based) liquid until the sauce reduces and the flavor soaks deep into the food: 감자조림, 장조림 (soy-braised beef), 생선조림. The contrast pair is 조림 vs 찌개/전골: a 조림 ends up nearly dry with a thick, concentrated, salty glaze (you don't drink it), whereas stews keep plenty of broth. It's also distinct from 무침 (tossed raw, no heat). Because the soy seasoning is strong and reduced, 조림 is a salty, long-keeping 반찬. Beware a spelling trap: the cooking verb is 조리다 'braise down' (단모음 ㅗ), which Koreans themselves often misspell as 졸이다 — and note 졸이다 also separately means 'to fret/be anxious' (마음을 졸이다). Pitfall for learners: don't expect a soupy result; a finished 조림 has almost no liquid left.

Confusing 조림 (braised in reducing sauce, with heat) with 무침 (tossed raw by hand, no heat).

usage: 노릇하다 'golden-brown' — the look of good grilling
two servings of grilled pork belly
examples: 저는 생선구이를 좋아해요.
I like grilled fish.
simple preference statement
고등어구이가 노릇하게 잘 익었어요.
The grilled mackerel cooked up nicely golden.
everyday texture comment; -게 makes 노릇 adverbial
삼겹살은 노릇하게 구워서 쌈에 싸 먹어요.
Grill the pork belly golden, then wrap it in lettuce to eat.
real BBQ scene; 굽다→구워서 the ㅂ-irregular verb
nuance: 구이 is from 굽다 'to grill/roast' and names any dish defined by grilling over heat, attaching to the food: 생선구이, 고등어구이, 삼겹살구이, 더덕구이. It labels the cooking METHOD, in contrast to plain ingredient words like 고기 'meat' or 생선 'fish' (which say nothing about how it's cooked), and against 볶음 (stir-fried in a pan with oil and stirring) — 구이 is grilled/roasted, often with little or no oil and not constantly stirred. The signature golden-done word is 노릇하다 'golden-brown'. A key verb note: 굽다 'to grill' is a ㅂ-irregular verb, so the stem ㅂ becomes 우 — 굽다 → 구워요, 구웠어요, 구워서 — which is exactly where the noun 구이 comes from. Pitfall: don't use 구이 for boiled, steamed, or pan-fried food; reserve it for genuinely grilled/roasted dishes, and conjugate the verb as 구워- not '굽어-'.

english: jeongol; hot pot cooked at the table
usage: the hot pot comes to a boil
끓다 'boil' — it cooks in front of you
인분 servings; 전골 is ordered by portions to share
examples: 회식 때 다 같이 전골을 먹었어요.
At the work dinner we all ate hot pot together.
simple group context
전골이 보글보글 끓으면 드세요.
Eat once the hot pot is bubbling away.
everyday cue; 보글보글 mimetic for gentle bubbling
버섯전골 이 인분 시키고 사리 추가할게요.
We'll order mushroom hot pot for two and add a noodle refill.

The signature cognate phrase is 부침개를 부치다 'pan-fry a pancake', the texture word is 바삭하다 'crispy', and culturally it's rainy-day comfort food eaten with 막걸리 (rice wine). nuance: 백반 is Sino-Korean 白飯 — 白 'white' + 飯 'cooked rice' — literally 'white rice', but as a menu word it means the whole cheap home-style set: a bowl of rice with soup and a generous spread of small 반찬 side dishes, all decided by the kitchen. The contrast to learn is 백반 vs 정식: a 백반 is humble, side-dish-driven, and has no single fixed 'main' (you just get whatever the kitchen made that day), whereas a 정식 'set meal' is built around a named main dish (불고기정식) at a set price and feels more put-together. It evokes a Korean home-cooked tray, served in small neighborhood 식당 'eateries'. Count the whole spread with 상 'table setting'. Pitfall: don't take the literal 白飯 'white rice' meaning — ordering 백반 does NOT get you a plain bowl of rice; it gets you a full meal — and don't expect to choose your sides, since 백반 comes pre-set by the cook.
